title: AgentDesk
pitch: A capability-virtualization runtime that gives WebMCP agents the right tools at the right time—with human approval, receipts, and rollback for consequential actions.
about_excerpt: A capability-virtualization runtime that gives WebMCP agents the right tools at the right time—with human approval, receipts, and rollback for consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Desk Inspiration WebMCP gives websites a direct, typed way to work with agents. But a production application may contain dozens or hundreds of operations. Publishing all of them at once creates a flat, expensive tool surface, makes selection less reliable, and places dangerous actions beside harmless reads. AgentDesk started from a simple question: what if the WebMCP tool registry behaved like a task-aware interface instead of a static API dump? What it does AgentDesk is a capability-virtualization and governance runtime for WebMCP applications. The Meridian Ops demo contains 79 internal capabilities across customers, orders, inventory, shipping, billing, support, and reports. The agent initially sees only four bootstrap tools. When it describes a task, AgentDesk: ranks the catalog against the task and current application context; dynamically registers up to five relevant, typed WebMCP tools; retires stale tools while leaving structured tombstones for clients with cached tool lists; explains unavailable actions and suggests what can make them possible; separates reads, ordinary writes, and consequential actions; returns approval-required immediately for consequential work instead of leaving a tool call hanging; shows the human an exact before/after preview; executes only after human approval and re-checks state at commit time; returns durable receipts describing what actually changed; supports reviewable multi-step plans, idempotency, verification, rollback, and human reconciliation when an outcome cannot be proven. Guided execution keeps the agent and person in the same application: tool calls navigate to, reveal, and highlight the affected object while the structured result remains authoritative. A Baseline mode exposes the full catalog so judges can compare the two approaches using the same tasks and data. Why WebMCP is essential This experience depends on the page and the agent sharing one live application context. AgentDesk registers tools directly with document.modelContext ; the browser page owns capability state, approval UI, and the visible business data. A server-only MCP integration cannot provide the same shared attention, dynamic page-scoped registry, or approval card beside the exact value being changed. The result is a collaboration model that was difficult before: the agent can move quickly through structured operations while the human sees the affected state, governs consequential decisions, and receives proof afterward. How we built it The judged path is a TypeScript SDK, @agentdesk/webmcp , with no backend, database, model API, or external runtime service. A document-lifetime runtime owns the catalog, deterministic router, availability checks, policy engine, approvals, plans, audit events, receipts, and persistence. A single ToolSurfaceManager publishes capabilities through the WebMCP adapter; React only observes runtime state and renders the product experience. Dynamic retirement uses abort signals and tombstone tools. A stable invoke_capability gateway covers clients whose discovery lags behind registry changes. Evidence is detached and frozen at system boundaries. Idempotency claims occur before dispatch, and any post-dispatch uncertainty becomes an explicit indeterminate state rather than a fabricated success or safe retry. We also built a real-browser P0 harness that exercises native registration, same-turn dynamic tools, retirement, stale calls, re-registration, typed execution, approvals, and compatibility behavior. Challenges The hardest work was not registering a tool—it was making stateful tool lifecycles honest under retries, reloads, stale client snapshots, approval delays, partial failures, and interrupted rollback. We repeatedly tested the boundaries where a system is tempted to overclaim: whether a write actually landed, whether a rollback truly restored prior state, whether evidence can be mutated, whether a repeated call can execute twice, and whether a benchmark accidentally rewards AgentDesk by construction. Those failures now have explicit domain states and regression tests. Accomplishments A working, WebMCP-native SDK rather than a one-page integration A complete operations product spanning seven business domains Task-scoped dynamic tool registration over a 79-capability catalog Human approval with visual diffs and post-action receipts Governed multi-step plans exposed through WebMCP Guided execution that keeps human attention aligned with agent actions A reproducible Baseline-versus-AgentDesk benchmark Live validation in the Codex in-app browser and Chrome 152 with WebMCP enabled An open-source MIT-licensed repository and static public deployment What we learned The registry itself can be an interaction surface. Registering, retiring, and rewriting capabilities based on task and state gives an agent clearer affordances than another layer of prompting. We also learned that governance needs more than a confirmation modal: it needs explicit acting identity, execution-time re-checks, idempotency, evidence, and a truthful representation of unknown outcomes. What's next AgentDesk can become an adoption layer for complex web applications: generated capabilities from existing application schemas, runtime-configurable routing, durable cross-session reconciliation, application adapters, and a browser extension that helps legacy sites expose governed WebMCP capabilities. The same model applies beyond operations software to editors, design tools, IDEs, and admin platforms. video_transcript_excerpt: AI agents can operate websites, but giving them every available tool creates confusion, risk, and unnecessary context. Agent desk turns web MCP capabilities into governed workflows. It reveals only the tools relevant to the current task while keeping consequential actions under human control. Here, a crew is stranded aboard Asteria. The agent discovers the mission state and prepares one rescue plan. Reserve oxygen, assign the drone, reroute power, and launch. These are real staged operations, not a description written by the agent. Agent desk derives the proposed changes from the application's own state. Nothing launches until a person authorizes the complete plan. After approval, every operation executes once, is verified, and produces evidence. The mission completes and the crew is recovered. The rescue interface is only one demonstration. The same agent desk runtime works inside an ordinary business application without changing its governance model. This application contains 79 capabilities. For Alice Johnson's shipping request, agent desk routes the task and exposes only five relevant tools. The agent finds Alice's unshipped order, confirms that she paid an $18 shipping fee, and proposes a refund. Because the refund changes customer and financial state, execution stops at a visible approval boundary. The human sees the exact impact before deciding. After approval, agent desk performs the refund once and verifies the result against live application state. The final evidence connects the operation to its consequences. Shipping is refunded, the customer receives an $18 credit, and the invoice becomes partially refunded. This governance also improves efficiency. The baseline exposes 79 tools and 28,894 bytes of schemas. Agent desk uses five tools and 3,776 bytes. 93.7% fewer tools and 86.9% less schema. Agent desk makes browser agents focused, observable, and safe enough to trust.

live_observation.first_impression: Meridian Ops presents an operations dashboard with navigation for customers, orders, inventory, shipping, billing, support, and reports. A prominent Route a Task control and recent orders make the capability-governance purpose apparent.
live_observation.action_attempted: Entered 'Find ticket T-2009' in Task to route and clicked Route.
live_observation.after_state: A ROUTING DECISION section appeared while the dashboard remained visible; the task text stayed in the input. No detailed decision text was exposed in the interactive snapshot.
live_observation.notes: The demo visibly supports task routing and shows an activity area.
